description: We’re a two-person team combining Product Design and Embedded Systems. One focuses on UI/UX, Figma and SwiftUI; the other on Embedded C/C++, ESP32, robotics, sensors and PCB design. For Martian Map, we aim to build an interactive Mars exploration experience that makes scientific data clear and useful. We’re looking for teammates with GIS, astronomy, data science or backend skills.
summary: Stargazing Martian is an interactive, layered atlas of Mars that helps a human explorer plan a Mars-walk. Robots have already walked Mars for us, so instead of inventing routes we start from ground truth: every rover traverse NASA has published (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance, 138 km in total) is placed on a 3D globe, split into science phases and scored for how hard each part would be on foot. Difficulty comes from the rover’s own measured tilt or from incidents in the mission record, and each segment explains why it is easy, medium or hard. Around these routes we layer NASA science: MOLA topography, TES dust and surface temperature, a radiation-shielding proxy, Pancam observations and NASA photos with 360° panoramas. A planet-wide network of 45 expedition corridors links landing sites and science destinations as least-cost paths over slope, temperature and radiation. It matters because the first crews will need one trustworthy map that brings scattered mission data together, shows where the ground is hard, and is honest about its limits before anyone sets foot on Mars.
details:
What it does and how it works
Stargazing Martian is a layered, interactive Mars atlas for planning a Mars-walk. It opens with a 3D globe (CesiumJS) built from NASA imagery and a static 3D terrain package. Scroll to explore, and 11 pins mark the landing sites of 12 missions, from Viking 1 to Perseverance and Ingenuity.

Selecting a rover shows its real traverse: Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance, 138 km in total. Each traverse is split into 19 science-phase segments and coloured green, orange or red by how hard it would be to walk. For Curiosity and Perseverance, difficulty comes from the rover’s own measured tilt at every stop. For Spirit and Opportunity, which logged no tilt, it comes from mission-record incidents such as the Purgatory dune and Troy. Every segment explains its rating. Relief switches to 5× around the selected site so the terrain reads clearly. Mission cards show NASA photos and full-screen 360° panoramas.

A map-mode panel switches between Terrain, Topography (MOLA), Atmospheric Dust and Surface Temperature (MGS TES), and a Radiation-shielding proxy (NASA/JSC HZETRN study). A “Mission and time” view shows historical MER Pancam atmospheric opacity by Sol or date.

Beyond the rovers, a planet-wide network of 45 expedition corridors links landing sites and science destinations such as Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris and Hellas. The corridors are least-cost paths over MOLA slope and roughness, TES temperature and the radiation proxy. Each one reports distance, climb, slope, coldest temperature and the number of sols a rover expedition would need.

Benefits and intended impact
Mission data is scattered across many NASA archives. We bring it into one map that a non-specialist can read in seconds: where the ground is easy or hard, why, and what conditions to expect. Mission planners, students and the public can explore Mars through the lens of a human explorer. The long-term goal is to grow this into a planning tool for the first crews, adding EVA limits, live weather and NASA’s candidate human landing zones.

Tools and technologies

  • Front end: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS, with CesiumJS for the 3D globe and Pannellum for panoramas.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy and scikit-image.
  • 3D terrain: CTOD (Cesium Terrain on Demand) with Docker, from the USGS HRSC/MOLA DEM.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages.
  • NASA data: MMGIS, PDS MER Analyst’s Notebook, MOLA MEGDR, MGS TES, MER Pancam, Mars Trek (Viking, CTX) and the NASA Image Library.

What makes it creative
Instead of drawing hypothetical routes, we reuse the routes robots have actually driven and read them through an astronaut’s eyes. Rover telemetry becomes walking difficulty, and real incidents become warnings. A Google Maps-style experience (pins, routes, segments, a road network) makes planetary science feel familiar and explorable.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about limits. Orbital data cannot see boulders, small craters or cliffs, and rover tilt is only a proxy for slope. We label every result as a planning aid, not a verified safe route.
  • Data provenance. Source vertices are preserved, and every layer names its source.
  • Accessibility and performance. Colour is never the only cue, so text labels accompany it. The site loads without a backend, the UI is English-only, and it works in any modern browser.
  • Licensing. NASA public-domain data and imagery, with the HRSC CC BY-SA terms credited in About.

Live site: https://stargazing-martian.github.io/StargazingMartian/
